plan: Retained: Prava slides a laminated org chart across the desk and tells Milo that his skills are a strong culture fit. Milo, who has never been told his boredom was valuable, feels seen and agrees before anyone asks. He goes from newly dead to employed.

Read the Appendices: At the next desk in Reconciliations, Zara tells him to read the appendices and thank no one. Milo hears it as mentorship and pitches trackers and quick wins at her. She gives him one rule: close what is in his queue and open nothing else. The rule plants the first boundary he will later cross.

Four Minutes: The Bell account arrives. Milo zeroes Halvard Bell's tenure, initials the form, and Bell is sent under by lunch while Facilities clears his desk. Milo's eager question about where Bell goes gets only 'He goes under' from Zara and a remark from Old Fen that nobody reads the appendices. Milo is unsettled for the first time, though he could not say why.
The Drawer: That night Milo locks the ledger in his desk drawer, which nobody asked him to do. It is his first act of keeping something back from the Pipeline.

The Memo: A heavy memo signed by Edric Thane summons Milo personally. Milo takes it as a career signal. Zara tells him it is not normal: bring nothing, sign nothing, and stand if offered a chair. Her warning is the first time she has openly taken his side.

Appetite: In the cold corner office the Lich invites Milo to sit, and Milo, to his own surprise, stays standing. Edric names Milo's four-minute close of the Bell account as appetite rather than diligence, and warns that the reason Milo was retained is not the reason he will be kept. Milo leaves knowing he is being watched and measured.

Moved, Not Zeroed: Milo unlocks his drawer and finds that, in a column nobody has explained to him, Bell's tenure was moved rather than zeroed. Bringing it to Zara as a discrepancy in search of a stakeholder, he hears her say he has finally read an appendix and should sit down because they have paperwork to do. Milo goes from obedient clerk to someone who knows.

Ink That Shows Under Grief: Zara gives Milo the full contract, appendices included, and teaches him to read the clauses printed in ink that shows only under grief. Their lessons change from training in closing accounts to training in noticing.

Following the Column: Milo requests old closed files from Records, where Old Fen hands them over without curiosity, and runs the moved-tenure column back through every restructured account. All of it flows upward into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. A suspicion becomes a sum.

Everything Else Is Overhead: Milo names it aloud to Zara: the souls sent under are not destroyed but harvested, their hope funneled upward to keep Edric Thane continuing. The harvest is not a side effect of the business; it is the business. Milo's picture of his job, and of himself as good at it, collapses.

The Draft: Milo's reflex takes over and he begins a crisp memo reporting the discrepancy upward, already imagining being seen and promoted. Zara reads it over his shoulder and says nothing, letting him write it. The temptation to climb as Edric once did is now on paper.

Eleven Thousand Names: Milo returns to the intake atrium and finds that Prava remembers every soul she has onboarded and keeps their names in a private ledger she is not permitted to have, Halvard Bell's among them. The harvested souls stop being account numbers to him.

Content: Milo watches Old Fen filing himself into Records, envies his contentment, and then watches the cheerful Retention team talk a wavering soul back onto schedule. He sees what he becomes if he stays good at his job, and envy turns to fear.

Confetti That Dissolves: At the all-hands graduation in the bedrock amphitheater, the quarter's single graduate leaves to applause and Prava weeps off the clock. Milo realizes that the Lich, the one soul ever able to buy the onward, chose to stay, and that the owner of the machine does not believe in its product.

In: Back at his desk, Milo cannot stand the memo or the version of himself who wrote it. He tears it up and tells Zara he is in. She offers him her alternative: not a rebellion but a union of the dead and a procedurally impeccable work stoppage. Milo is no longer climbing; he is organized.

The Signature Sheet: Zara takes a signature sheet from department to department. Prava signs first and offers her forbidden ledger of eleven thousand names as the membership roll. Even Old Fen, after a long pause, files his own name. The dead stop being alone, which is the one thing the curve was built to prevent.

Starting With Bell: Milo reopens the Bell account and reconciles it correctly, restoring Halvard Bell's tenure line by line under the Pipeline's own rules, then works through every soul ever sent under. The speed the Lich called appetite now runs in reverse.

Restructuring the Account at the Top: Milo files the restructuring of Edric Thane's pooled account through Reconciliations, the department built to close accounts. Zara checks every field twice, because the Lich can survive a threat but not a correctly filed contradiction. The undoing becomes a document waiting for review.

Reply All: The work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest about what the Pipeline does, and the Marrow District stops hoping on schedule. A memo comes back summoning Milo to a quarterly review. The confrontation is now set.

Stand: Milo enters the corner office, is offered a chair again and stands, this time on purpose. He hands Edric Thane a single sheet: his own resignation, with the procedurally flawless reconciliation of every soul ever sent under attached. The power in the room passes from the reviewer to the reviewed.

Files It Correctly: Edric reads it the way a clerk reads, recognizes his younger self in Milo, and finds no error. Undone by a clerk under his own terms of service, he initials the reconciliation, his pooled account zeroes, and he goes onward, the thing he spent six centuries afraid of.

Plain Language: Back in Reconciliations, Milo's boredom returns and he understands it was never a personality but a wound where his questions used to be. Zara, after two centuries of anger, has company. The Undeath Pipeline must now explain to its customers, in plain language, what it does.

beats: Milo opens his eyes in the gray, windowless intake atrium, mid-thought about a meeting that could have been an email, and finds himself seated at a laminate desk, disoriented but already reaching for the composure he uses in meetings.

A caseworker whose lanyard reads PRAVA greets him by name with practised, unhurried warmth and slides a laminated org chart across the desk. She is so kind that Milo relaxes before he can wonder how she already knows him.

Prava tells him he has been retained, that his skills are a strong culture fit and that he will start Monday in Reconciliations. Milo looks for his own box on the org chart, feels seen for the first time in decades, and hears his forty-one years of boredom called an asset.
Milo says yes, warmly and at once, before any question has been asked. In the half-beat before she smiles, he notices that no one had offered him a choice, and he lets the thought go.

On Monday Milo is shown to his desk in Reconciliations, a long room the colour of old teeth lit from nowhere, and finds a woman across the low partition whose nameplate reads Z. OKAFOR. She does not look up, and he takes her silence as a busy colleague's focus rather than a verdict.

Milo cheerfully mentions how kind the intake caseworker was, and Zara, still not looking up, tells him to read the appendices first, every one of them, and then thank no one. He hears a seasoned mentor's tough-love tip and files it under onboarding.

Encouraged, Milo rolls his chair toward the partition and pitches quick wins, throughput trackers and a shared doc. Zara's grey eyes rest on him for exactly one second, and the flatness of her answers keeps landing as jokes he laughs at alone.

Zara gives him the only rule she will give: close the accounts in his queue and do not open the ones that are not. Milo writes it down as though it were a KPI, satisfied to have a clear boundary and not curious about what lies past it.

plan: A Strong Culture Fit: Prava slides a laminated org chart across the desk and tells Milo he has been retained for Reconciliations; for the first time in decades he feels seen and useful, and he says yes before anyone offers him a choice.

Across the Partition: At his new desk Milo pitches throughput trackers and low-hanging fruit; Zara answers with flat instructions to close only his queue and read the appendices, and Milo mistakes her deadpan for a joke and her courtesy for friendship.

Four Minutes: The Bell account arrives; Milo zeroes ninety years of Halvard Bell's tenure, initials the form and watches Facilities clear Bell's desk before the coffee finishes dispensing, and when he asks where Bell goes Zara tells him to write 'under' and nothing else.

Nobody Reads the Appendices: Old Fen remarks without looking up that nobody reads the appendices, and that night Milo locks the ledger in his drawer without being asked, his first unexplained act of caution.

Paper With Its Own Gravity: A heavy memo signed by Edric Thane summons Milo, who reads it as a career win until Zara, unsmiling, tells him to bring nothing, sign nothing and stand if offered a chair, and his excitement acquires its first edge of fear.

An Analyst Who Stands: In the library-cold office the Lich invites Milo to sit, praises his four-minute close as appetite and warns that he was retained for not asking questions; Milo stays standing, surprising himself, and leaves knowing he has been noticed by the top of the org chart.

The Column Nobody Explained: Back at his desk Milo unlocks the ledger and finds, beneath his own initials on the Bell entry, a column showing Bell's tenure was never zeroed but moved; he turns to Zara with the word discrepancy, and she tells him to sit down because they have a great deal of paperwork to do.

Overtime Nobody Approved: Night after night Zara sets closed accounts in front of Milo and says only 'Again'; by the twentieth he can read the unexplained column without being told, and noticing stops feeling like a question and starts feeling like a skill.

A Man Who Files Himself: Milo goes to Records for archived contracts and finds Old Fen, perfectly content among his folders, who hands over the files without curiosity; Milo envies that peace, and Zara's silence on the walk back tells him it is the thing she fears most.

Top of the Org Chart: Milo maps every moved column onto one sheet and watches the lines converge on a single pooled account at the top of the org chart, held by Edric Thane; he understands that the souls sent under are not destroyed but harvested, and the clean ledger he loved becomes evidence.

Eleven Thousand Names: Milo seeks out Prava and learns she remembers every soul she has onboarded and keeps their names in a private ledger she is not permitted to have; the warmth that welcomed him turns out to be grief, and the dead in his own columns acquire names.

Confetti That Never Lands: At the all-hands in the bedrock amphitheater the quarter's one graduation is celebrated while the cheerful Retention team applaud like the most despairing souls in the building; Milo sees Prava weeping silently and realises the onward is advertised by the one being who chose not to take it.

The Report He Almost Filed: Milo drafts a memo flagging the discrepancy upward, already imagining being seen and promoted, while Zara watches and says nothing; reading it back, he hears Edric's voice in his own sentences and understands he is becoming the Lich's younger self.

A Signature Sheet: Milo deletes the memo; Zara slides a blank signature sheet across the partition and offers not a rebellion but a work stoppage, a union of the dead, and Milo signs first, choosing the harder turn.

Names for the Columns: Prava opens her forbidden ledger to Milo, and her eleven thousand remembered names let him match every moved column to a soul; the reconciliation stops being numbers and becomes a roll call.

Clipboards at the Coffee Station: Milo watches Zara pass signature sheets desk to desk, from Retention's cheerful despair to Records, where even Old Fen, after a long pause, signs in perfect filing hand; the curve that kept the dead afraid alone gives way to a list of names that grows longer than any one soul's fear.

Form R-1, Restructuring: Milo completes the reconciliation of every soul ever sent under and, using the department's own forms, files the restructuring of Edric Thane's pooled account through Reconciliations; for the first time his gift for clean paperwork points against the machine instead of for it.

Reply All: Zara hits send on an all-staff email that announces the work stoppage in plain language, and Milo watches the room stop working, desk by desk, until the Pipeline falls silent and the newsletter, for once, has nothing to say.

A Single Sheet of Paper: Summoned to his review, Milo again declines the chair and hands Edric Thane his resignation with the reconciliation attached, Halvard Bell's restored tenure on its first line; the clerk who once wanted to be seen by the Lich now makes the Lich read.

The Terms of Service: Edric checks every figure and finds no error; he speaks of six centuries of continuance and his fear of the onward, and Milo watches the most powerful being in the afterlife recognise himself in the clerk standing before him.

Filed Correctly: Edric initials the restructuring of his own account, files it in the proper tray and is gone, the pooled account zeroed by the rules he enforced; Milo is left alone in the one office no one returns from unchanged, and walks out changed.

Plain Language: Back in Reconciliations the Pipeline sends its first honest notice explaining what it does; Milo sits beside Zara with nothing urgent in his queue, finally bored in a way that no longer feels like a wound, and Zara, for once, looks up and stays.

On Monday Milo arrives in Reconciliations, a long room the colour of old teeth lit from nowhere, and finds his new desk facing a woman across a low partition who does not look up; he takes her silence for focus and admires it.

Milo introduces himself and learns her name is Zara Okafor; she turns flat grey eyes on him for exactly one second, tells him to close the accounts in his queue and not to open the ones that aren't, and goes back to her screen, which Milo hears as a crisp onboarding brief.

Rolling his chair closer, Milo pitches a throughput tracker and low-hanging fruit, citing the eleven percent cycle-time win that was the best week of his life, and Zara answers that it was the best week of his death too, he just hasn't had the others yet.

Milo laughs, certain it was a joke, and she does not; when she adds, without inflection, that he should read the appendices before he thanks anyone, he takes the instruction as a kindness and decides, warmly and wrongly, that they are going to be friends.

plan: A Meeting That Could Have Been an Email: Milo dies on a Tuesday, halfway through a sentence about a pointless meeting, and opens his eyes in the intake atrium of the Undeath Pipeline. He goes from irritated living employee to a disoriented new arrival holding a numbered ticket.

Strong Culture Fit: Prava slides a laminated org chart across her desk and tells him warmly that his forty-one years of optimisation make him a strong culture fit. Milo says yes to Reconciliations before anyone offers him a choice. He notices she writes his name in a small private notebook that is not the official form, but his overriding feeling is that someone has finally seen him.

Sometimes It's Quieter: Milo arrives in Reconciliations with a lanyard and a desk beside Zara Okafor, who trains him in short flat instructions and never looks up. He chatters, over-explains and asks eager questions, and she answers in single words. By the end of the shift he has closed his first restructured account cleanly and feels useful for the first time in decades, without asking where the account went.

Top of the Curve: A year on, Milo leads Reconciliations on quota and is praised in the newsletter, which everyone at the coffee station quietly agrees is the worst part. Zara asks him one flat question about where a closed account goes, and he answers cheerfully that it is not their workstream. His competence is now visibly a habit of not asking.

Confetti That Never Lands: At the all-hands in the bedrock amphitheatre, the quarter's single graduate is announced to dissolving confetti and Milo applauds sincerely. He sees Prava weeping silently at the edge of the crowd and is unsettled. A slide naming the CEL, Edric Thane, at the top of the org chart is the first time Milo realises the CEL is a person and not a department.

The Numbers Do Not Reconcile: Closing a routine restructured account, Milo finds the remaining tenure leaving the ledger faster than any labor could explain. He follows the transfers, still sure it is a clerical error he can fix, and finds every one routed into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. He asks Zara whether it is always like this, and she says, 'Look again.' The act ends with Milo unable to make the numbers balance.

A Man Filed Under F: Milo goes down to Records to pull source documents and finds Old Fen half-shelved among the cabinets, entirely at peace with it. Fen helps him cheerfully and does not ask why. Milo envies Fen's contentment and is frightened by it in equal measure, and he leaves with the transfer authorisations he came for.

Where Under Goes: Cross-referencing the authorisations, Milo can no longer read the transfers as an error. Each soul sent under has its accrued tenure drawn off and routed to the pooled account held by the CEL, Edric Thane. The souls are not destroyed but harvested, and he has been closing their accounts for a year. His understanding of his own excellent work turns over completely.

Executive Summary: Back at his desk, Milo starts drafting the finding as a report for Management, with bullet points, stakeholders and next steps, already picturing his name in the newsletter. Zara reads it over the partition and says only, 'Finish it.' The beat ends with Milo's first instinct exposed as the same climb that made the Lich.

A Retention Conversation: A flagged wobble in Milo's productivity earns him a session with Halvard Bell, once a dentist and now ninety years in Retention, who talks him gently back onto the schedule with practised cheer. Milo leaves reassured and then sees Bell sitting alone and motionless afterwards. He realises the man best at keeping souls hopeful has none left himself.

What Zara Keeps in the Bottom Drawer: Milo finishes the report and holds it out for Zara's approval. Without explaining, she opens her bottom drawer: two centuries of annotated contract appendices, names, departments and signatures, a union of the dead built one soul at a time. Milo sees that she has been recruiting him all along and that Reconciliations is the lever.

Delete, Sign: Milo sets his report beside the org chart, sees exactly where it would take him and who already stands at the top of that ladder, and deletes it. He signs Zara's sheet. She looks up at him for the first time. He has chosen the union of the dead over the climb Edric Thane once made.

Form 9-Stop, In Triplicate: Milo follows Zara from department to department as she gathers signatures for a work stoppage notice filed through every proper channel. Halvard Bell signs for Retention and, for the first time Milo has seen, does not smile. Old Fen does not sign, but he files the notice correctly so it cannot be lost. The stoppage stops being Zara's private project and becomes the workforce's.

Eleven Thousand Names: Milo cannot reconcile souls the Pipeline never recorded by name, and his plan stalls. Prava comes to his desk off the clock and hands him the private ledger she was not permitted to keep, holding every soul she has onboarded. With it, his reconciliation of everyone ever sent under can finally be completed.

The Line He Never Drew Down: Running the last figures, Milo and Zara see that the pooled account has never once paid out the graduation it was built to buy. Edric Thane earned the onward six hundred years ago and chose to continue instead. Milo puts it into words: the Lich does not believe in his own product, he is afraid of it, and that fear is the lever.

Summoned Upstairs: The stoppage notice reaches the top of the org chart and Milo is summoned to the office no employee returns from unchanged. At the lift Zara tells him, 'Don't explain. Hand it over.' Milo goes up alone with one sheet of paper and its attachment.

Mr. Voss: Edric Thane receives Milo with formal courtesy and tries to recruit him upward, offering the same climb he once made. Milo hands over his resignation with the reconciliation attached. Edric reads it, finds no error and sees that by his own rules his pooled account is zeroed and every harvested soul's tenure restored. He recognises in Milo the clerk he used to be.

Filed Correctly: Edric initials the box marked INITIAL HERE, files the closure of his own account correctly and goes onward in front of Milo, leaving an empty chair and a clean ledger. The Lich's continuance is over, and it ended in paperwork.

Plain Language: Back on the floor, Milo watches the all-staff email go out announcing the stoppage and stating, honestly and in plain language, what the Pipeline does. He sits down beside Zara with a gray coffee and nothing urgent to do. She does not look up, but she stays, and neither of them is alone.

beats: Mid-sentence on a Tuesday, Milo is telling a colleague that the morning's meeting could have been an email when the sentence simply stops, and the irritation he feels is the most alive thing about him.

He opens his eyes in a vast, windowless atrium under flat fluorescent light, still holding the rest of the sentence, and tries to take it as a reorg or an offsite before the quiet of it frightens him.
A dispenser by the entrance gives him a numbered paper ticket and a screen shows NOW SERVING a much lower number, and the familiar shape of a queue calms him more than it should.

Sitting in a molded plastic chair among other silent arrivals holding tickets, Milo notices he has no pulse to check, no phone and no hunger, and he decides, with a professional's relief, to wait until his number is called.

His number is called at last, and Milo sits down at a laminate desk whose nameplate reads PRAVA, INTAKE, across from a caseworker whose warmth is so practised and complete that it loosens him at once.

Prava slides a laminated org chart across the desk and goes through his forty-one years of optimisation as if they were achievements, calling him a strong culture fit, and Milo, who has never heard his boredom described as an asset, glows.

She mentions that Reconciliations has an opening starting Monday, and Milo says yes, eagerly and at length, before she has finished the sentence or offered him any choice, and she smiles as if this happens every time.

As she stamps his official form, Milo sees her also write his name carefully in a small worn notebook she keeps below the desk, which looks nothing like the paperwork, and he files the oddity away under the much larger feeling that someone has finally seen him.

On Monday Milo arrives on the Reconciliations floor with a new lanyard and is shown to a desk across a low partition from a woman who gives her name, Zara Okafor, without looking up, and his bright introduction falls into her silence like a coin into a well.

Zara trains him in short flat commands (open the queue, check the tenure, zero it, initial here) while Milo asks eager, over-explained questions about dashboards and best practice and gets single words back, and he takes her terseness for a kind of efficient friendliness.

At the coffee station Milo fills a chipped mug with something gray and tries small talk about the newsletter, and Zara's one dry, deadpan answer is funny enough that he laughs and cold enough that the laugh does not quite finish.

Near the end of the shift Milo closes his first restructured account: he zeroes the tenure, initials the box and watches the entry turn gray and disappear from his queue, and the clean click of it makes him feel useful for the first time in decades while the question of where it went never forms.

BORED TO UNDEATH — a synopsis

PART ONE: THE FIRM

Death, it turns out, is not an ending but an onboarding.

When the world's largest afterlife-services conglomerate, Aeon Holdings, quietly
won the exclusive concession to process the recently deceased three centuries
ago, no one living noticed, because no one living was the customer. The customers
arrived already dead, disoriented, and — crucially — in no position to read the
terms of service. Aeon's founding insight was elegant and terrible: a soul, freed
from the friction of a body, is the most efficient labor unit ever devised. It
does not sleep. It does not unionize, historically speaking. It does not age out
of usefulness, because it has already aged out of everything. It simply needs to
be told what to do, and given the faint, renewable hope that doing it well might
one day earn a promotion out of the ledger and into whatever lies beyond the
beyond.

That hope is the product. That hope is the whole business.

Aeon calls its core operation the Undeath Pipeline, and in the internal style
guide the term is always capitalized, always singular, and never — under any
circumstances — described in plain language to a new hire. The Pipeline is the
machinery by which raw grief is refined into shareholder value: intake,
orientation, assignment, extraction, and, for the vanishingly few, "graduation."
Most of the dead never learn what the Pipeline actually pipes, or where. They
learn their department. They learn their quota. They learn the difference between
a billable haunting and a non-billable one, and they learn not to ask what
happens to the souls whose contracts are "restructured."

The afterlife economy runs on a single currency, called tenure, which is accrued
by labor and spent on the only thing the dead still want: the possibility of
moving on. You cannot buy tenure. You cannot steal it, though people try. You can
only earn it, quarter by quarter, in the gray fluorescent light of the Marrow
District, the vast subterranean office park where the Pipeline's clerical work is
done. The Marrow District has no windows, because there is nothing outside it to
see, and no clocks, because time is a benefit reserved for management.

There is a culture to the place, and the culture is the cruelest technology Aeon
ever built. New hires are given a lanyard, a desk, and a mentor, and the mentor is
always someone three quarters of the way to burning out, because a soul who still
believes is a poor teacher of resignation. There are all-hands meetings, held in
an amphitheater carved from a single slab of the bedrock beneath the Marrow
District, at which the quarter's graduation — always exactly one, always announced
with confetti that dissolves before it lands — is celebrated as proof that the
system works. There are performance reviews, calibrated on a curve so that
someone must always be failing, so that the fear is evenly distributed and never
pools into anything as dangerous as solidarity. There are team-building
exercises. There is a newsletter. The newsletter is the worst part, and everyone
agrees, quietly, at the coffee station that dispenses a gray liquid the dead drink
out of habit rather than need, that the newsletter is the worst part, and no one
ever says so where it could be documented.

The departments spread out from the Pipeline like rings of a felled tree.
Intake greets the newly dead and sorts them by exploitable virtue. Orientation
teaches them the vocabulary that will keep them from ever describing their
situation accurately. Assignment matches a soul's dearest surviving habit to the
task that will grind it down most efficiently: the meticulous go to Records, the
loyal go to Retention, the curious — the dangerous, curious ones — go to
Reconciliations, where curiosity is spent closing the accounts of the disappeared
until there is none left. Above them all floats Management, a stratum of the dead
so thoroughly graduated-in-spirit that they no longer remember wanting to leave,
and above Management, alone, the office at the top.

At the very top of Aeon Holdings sits an office that no employee has ever
entered and returned from unchanged. The being who occupies it holds a title so
old that it has worn down, through centuries of memos and org charts and
mandatory compliance trainings, into a three-letter abbreviation that new hires
mistake, understandably, for the name of a subsidiary or a line of business. They
hear "the CEL" and they picture a department — Corporate something, Logistics
something — and they are not corrected, because the misunderstanding is useful.
The CEL is not a department. The CEL is a person, or was one, a very long time
ago. The letters stand for Chief Executive Lich, and the Lich is real, and the
Lich is watching the numbers.

This is a story about three of the dead, and about what happens to a machine
built on hope when the people inside it finally, quietly, stop hoping.

PART TWO: THE NEW HIRE

Milo Voss died the way most people do: unremarkably, mid-sentence, on a Tuesday,
while complaining about a meeting that could have been an email. In life he had
been a mid-level operations analyst for a company that made a component that went
into a component that went into something no one could name, and he had been, by
his own cheerful admission, extraordinarily good at a job that did not matter. He
had spent forty-one years optimizing processes whose purpose he never questioned,
and he had been comfortable, and he had been bored, and the boredom had felt, at
the time, like a personality.

So when Milo Voss opened his eyes in the intake atrium of the Undeath Pipeline
and a caseworker slid a laminated org chart across a laminate desk and explained,
in the warm and terrible voice of onboarding everywhere, that he had been
retained, that his skills were a strong culture fit, and that he would be
starting Monday in Reconciliations — Milo felt something he had not felt in
decades. He felt seen. He felt, God help him, useful. The afterlife had looked at
his forty-one years of pointless optimization and decided they were an asset, and
Milo Voss, who had never in his life or death been told that his boredom was
valuable, said yes before anyone thought to offer him a choice.

It takes him the better part of a fiscal year to understand what he has agreed
to. Reconciliations, he learns, is the department that closes the accounts of
souls whose contracts have been restructured — that reviews their remaining
tenure, zeroes it out, and files the paperwork that sends them not onward, but
under, into the part of the Pipeline that the style guide will not name. Milo has
been hired, on the strength of his gift for not asking questions, to be very good
at the one job in the afterlife that ought to require asking every question there
is. And he is good at it. That is the horror of the middle of this book: Milo Voss
is good at it, and he likes being good at it, and the liking lasts almost until
the end.

PART THREE: THE ORGANIZER

Zara Okafor has been dead for two hundred and six years, and she has spent almost
all of them angry.

She died young, in a factory fire that the living world found regrettable and the
Pipeline found routine, and she arrived in the Marrow District with the one trait
Aeon Holdings has never found a way to refine out of a soul: she could not stop
noticing who was getting hurt. Two centuries of noticing have made her the most
dangerous kind of employee — the kind who has read the entire contract, including
the appendices, including the parts printed in the ink that only shows up under
grief. Zara knows what the Pipeline pipes. She has known for a hundred years. What
she has never had is leverage, because a soul alone has none, and the dead, Aeon
has made very sure, are always alone.

Zara Okafor is Milo's desk neighbor. She is assigned to train him, and she does,
flawlessly, with a flat professional courtesy that Milo mistakes for friendship
and then, slowly, comes to understand is something far more patient and far more
frightening: recruitment. Zara has spent decades identifying the one structural
weakness in the Undeath Pipeline, and it is not a vault or a password or a
weapon. It is a job. It is Reconciliations. Whoever controls the department that
closes the accounts controls the one ledger the Lich actually reads. And Zara has
just been handed a brand-new Reconciliations analyst who is lonely, and gifted,
and bored, and who has no idea yet that he is the most important soul in the
building.

PART FOUR: THE LICH IN THE CORNER OFFICE

Edric Thane was the third son of a minor merchant house, and he was, in life, a
clerk. This is the joke the whole novel is built on and the reason it aches: the
most powerful being in the afterlife, the Chief Executive Lich, the CEL whose
initials terrify every new hire, was once exactly what Milo Voss is now. Edric
Thane died six hundred years ago owing a debt he could not pay, and he was
retained, and he was good at it, and he was ambitious in the specific, grinding,
upward way of a man who has decided that the only escape from a machine is to
own it. He climbed. He reconciled. He restructured. He learned that tenure could
be pooled, and that a soul who controlled enough pooled tenure could purchase
something no clerk was ever meant to have: continuance. Edric Thane did not
graduate out of the Pipeline. He devoured it, and wore it, and became the reason
no one else ever would.

Now he sits at the top of Aeon Holdings, neither living nor properly dead, a
clerk's resentment scaled up to the size of an institution, and he is not cruel
so much as he is thorough. Edric Thane believes, with the total conviction of the
converted, that hope is a renewable resource and that spending it is what it is
for. He is the villain of this book, and he is right about almost everything, and
that is what makes him terrible: he was Milo once. He was Zara's colleague once.
He is what the Pipeline is designed to produce, the one graduate it will permit,
and his continued existence is the proof, filed and notarized, that the way out
is real — for exactly one soul, and never again.

PART FIVE: THE RESTRUCTURING

The plot turns on a routine account. Milo Voss, closing the books on a soul whose
contract has been restructured, notices — because Zara Okafor has spent a year
teaching him, gently, to notice — that the numbers do not reconcile. Tenure is
disappearing from the ledger faster than labor can explain, and it is all flowing
to a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. Milo has found, without
looking for it, the mechanism by which the CEL sustains himself: every soul
"sent under" is not destroyed but harvested, their accrued hope funneled upward to
keep one ancient clerk continuing. The Undeath Pipeline is not a business with a
monstrous side effect. The monstrous side effect is the business. Everything else
is overhead.

What Milo does with this knowledge is the spine of the back half of the book. His
first instinct — his forty-one years of instinct, his six-hundred-years-ago
Edric Thane instinct — is to optimize it. To report the discrepancy, to be
useful, to be seen, to climb. Zara lets him sit with that instinct until he
cannot stand himself, and then she offers him the alternative she has spent two
centuries building toward: not a rebellion, not a war, nothing so loud that the
Lich could file it under threat and restructure it away. A work stoppage. A
union of the dead. The one thing a machine that runs on hope cannot survive is
the coordinated, documented, procedurally impeccable refusal of its workforce to
keep hoping on schedule.

They do it the only way that could possibly work: as paperwork. Zara has the
organizing; Milo has the ledger; and between them they turn the CEL's own
bureaucracy into the instrument of his undoing, filing the restructuring of Edric
Thane's account through the very department built to close accounts. The climax is
not a battle. It is a quarterly review. Milo Voss stands in the one office no
employee returns from unchanged and hands the Chief Executive Lich a single sheet
of paper — a resignation, his own, and attached to it, procedurally flawless, the
reconciliation of every soul the Pipeline ever sent under, tenure restored, hope
returned, the pooled account that keeps Edric Thane continuing zeroed out by the
same rules Edric spent six centuries enforcing.

Edric Thane, who was a clerk, is undone by a clerk, according to the terms of
service, and the terrible mercy of the ending is that he understands it
completely, and files it correctly, and goes wherever it is the dead go when they
are finally, at last, allowed to be bored no longer.

The dead do not overthrow Aeon Holdings. That would be a different, easier book.
They do something quieter and harder: they read the contract to the end, together,
and hold the machine to its own word. Milo Voss gets his boredom back, and learns
it was never a personality — it was a wound where his questions used to be. Zara
Okafor gets the one thing two centuries of anger never could: company. And the
Undeath Pipeline, for the first time in three hundred years, has to explain to
its customers, in plain language, exactly what it is that it does.

PART SIX: THE PEOPLE IN THE MARGINS

The book is populated, in its middle chapters, by the small and specific dead who
give the satire its ache. There is Prava, the intake caseworker who onboarded
Milo with such practiced warmth and who, it emerges, has onboarded eleven thousand
souls and remembers the name of every one, and keeps them in a private ledger she
is not permitted to have, and weeps, silently and off the clock, at each
graduation because it is the only proof she has that leaving is possible. There is
Old Fen, who has been in Records so long that he has begun to file himself, whose
tragedy is that he is content, whose contentment is the thing Zara most fears and
Milo most envies. There is the Retention team, cheerful and doomed, whose job is
to talk the wavering out of despair and back onto the schedule, and who are very
good at it, and who are, without exception, the most despairing souls in the
building.

And there is the question the novel keeps in its pocket and never quite lets the
reader forget: what, exactly, is on the other side of graduation? Aeon promises an
"onward." The style guide will not define it. Edric Thane, the one soul to ever
buy his way past the ledger, chose not to take it — chose continuance in the
Marrow District over whatever the onward is — and that choice is the crack in the
Lich the whole plot slides a lever into. Because if graduation were truly the
reward the Pipeline sells, the most powerful being in the afterlife would have
taken it six hundred years ago. Edric Thane stayed. Edric Thane is afraid of the
onward. And a machine whose owner does not believe its own product is a machine
that can be brought down by anyone willing to read that fact out loud.

THEMES AND TEXTURE

At its heart, Bored to Undeath is a workplace comedy that curdles, by degrees,
into a tragedy about complicity — about how the most efficient evil is not the
kind that requires monsters but the kind that requires only competent, tired,
reasonable people who have agreed not to ask the next question. Milo Voss is not a
chosen one; he is a good employee, and the book's argument is that in a system
like the Pipeline those are the same thing until the moment they are not. Zara
Okafor is not a warrior; she is an organizer, and her weapon is not a sword but a
signature sheet, and the book insists, page after page, that this is the more
frightening thing to be, because a sword threatens the Lich and a signature sheet
threatens the terms of service, and the Lich can survive a threat but not a
correctly filed contradiction.

The tone is dry, deadpan, and specific: the horror is administrative, delivered in
the language of quarterly targets and culture fit and "restructuring," and the
comedy comes from the exact, lovingly observed gap between what the Pipeline says
it does and what it does. The undead here do not moan; they attend meetings. The
Lich does not roar; he reviews. The apocalypse, when it comes, comes as paperwork,
and the revolution, when it comes, comes as a work stoppage announced by an
all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest.

The setting — Aeon Holdings, the Undeath Pipeline, the windowless Marrow District,
the currency of tenure, the graduation that may be salvation or may be a nicer
word for the same disappearance — is the novel's central invention and its central
metaphor, and none of it should be flattened into a generic corporate dystopia,
because the specific joke is theological: this is what you get when an institution
designed to shepherd souls decides, quite reasonably, quite gradually, that the
souls are the inventory. The CEL is not a brand. The Pipeline is not a factory.
Milo and Zara and Edric are not archetypes wearing office clothes. They are three
clerks, six centuries apart, discovering the same terrible fork in the same gray
hallway, and choosing, two of them, at last, the harder turn.

Milo Voss opened his eyes in the intake atrium and a caseworker slid a laminated org chart across a laminate desk.

"You've been retained," she said, warmly. "Your skills are a strong culture fit. You'll be starting Monday in Reconciliations."

Zara Okafor, at the next desk, did not look up. "Don't thank her," she said. "Read the appendices first. Every one of them. Then thank no one."

Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth, lit from nowhere. Milo's desk faced Zara's across a low partition. Zara Okafor had grey eyes, flat as a filing cabinet, and she turned them on him for exactly one second before she went back to her screen.

"So!" Milo said, rolling his chair an inch closer to the partition. "Just so I'm aligned on expectations going in, what does a great first quarter look like here? Because I am very much a hit-the-ground-running person, and I'd love to circle back on any low-hanging fruit you've been meaning to get to."

"Close the accounts in your queue," Zara said. "Don't open the ones that aren't."

"Totally, totally. And is there a dashboard, or a tracker, or some kind of shared doc where we log throughput? I only ask because in my last role I built a tracker that cut our cycle time by eleven percent, which, honestly, was the best week of my life."

"It was the best week of your death, too. You just haven't had the others yet."

He laughed, because he thought it was a joke. She did not.

On Tuesday the Bell account came across Milo's queue. Halvard Bell had been a dentist, then a soul in Retention for ninety years, and his contract had been restructured at nine that morning. Milo zeroed the tenure, initialled the form, and by lunch Halvard Bell had been sent under. Facilities cleared his desk before the coffee station had finished dispensing.

"That's it?" Milo asked. "Where does he actually go? Not in a weird way. I'm just trying to understand the end-to-end process, because if I don't know the downstream impact I can't really optimize the upstream workflow, you know?"

Zara set down her pen. "He goes under. Write that on the form. Nothing else."

"Nobody reads the appendices," said Old Fen, without looking up from his filing. "That's what they're for."

Milo locked the ledger in his desk drawer that night, which no one had asked him to do, and he could not have said why he did it.

Two days after the Bell account, on Thursday, the memo arrived. It was printed on paper so heavy it seemed to have its own gravity, and it was signed in a hand that had practised the same signature for six hundred years: Edric Thane, Chief Executive.

Milo read it twice. "He wants to meet me. Personally. Is that normal? That feels like a really positive signal, career-wise."

"It is not normal," said Zara. "Bring nothing. Sign nothing. If he offers you a chair, stand."

The corner office was cold in the way that libraries are cold. Edric Thane sat behind a desk with nothing on it but a single ledger, closed, and his hands folded on top of it as if it might try to leave.

"Mr. Voss," the Lich said. "Do sit. One finds that a new analyst who stands is an analyst who intends to leave early, and leaving early is, in my experience, the most expensive habit a soul can acquire."

"I'm good, thanks," said Milo, and remained standing. He was surprised to hear himself say it.

Edric Thane opened the ledger without looking at it. "You closed the Bell account in under four minutes. I have read the figures. Four minutes is not diligence, Mr. Voss; four minutes is appetite. I was once possessed of the same appetite, and I have had six centuries in which to learn what it costs and who, in the end, pays."

"With respect, sir, I just like a clean ledger."

"Every clerk likes a clean ledger. It is the clerk who asks why the ledger is clean who becomes interesting to me."

"Is that a good thing? Being interesting?"

"Let us speak plainly, since you will not sit," said Edric. "You were retained because you do not ask questions. Do not mistake that for the reason you will be kept."

"Is there a reason I'll be kept?"

"There is always a reason, Mr. Voss, and it is always recorded, and it is never the one the soul in question would have chosen."

Back at his desk Milo unlocked his desk drawer and took out the ledger. The Bell entry was there in his own handwriting. Below it, in a column no one had ever explained to him, Bell's tenure had not been zeroed at all. It had been moved.

"Zara," he said. "Do you have a minute? I think I found a discrepancy, and I'm not totally sure who the right stakeholder is."

Zara looked at the column for a long time. Her grey eyes did not change at all.

"Now you've read an appendix," she said. "Sit down. We have a great deal of paperwork to do."

spans: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!

Welcome to my house. Come freely. Go safely; and leave something of the
happiness you bring!

I am Vasska; and I bid you welcome, Mr. Kerr, to my house. Come in;
the night air is chill, and you must need to eat and rest.

Nay, sir, you are my guest. It is late, and my people are not
available. Let me see to your comfort myself.

You will need, after your journey, to refresh yourself by making your
toilet. I trust you will find all you wish. When you are ready, come
into the other room, where you will find your supper prepared.

I pray you, be seated and sup how you please. You will, I trust, excuse
me that I do not join you; but I have dined already, and I do not sup.

I must regret that an attack of gout, from which malady I am a constant
sufferer, forbids absolutely any travelling on my part for some time to
come; but I am happy to say I can send a sufficient substitute, one in
whom I have every possible confidence. He is a young man, full of energy
and talent in his own way, and of a very faithful disposition. He is
discreet and silent, and has grown into manhood in my service. He shall
be ready to attend on you when you will during his stay, and shall take
your instructions in all matters.
Listen to them--the children of the night. What music they make!

Ah, sir, you dwellers in the city cannot enter into the feelings of the
hunter.
I have to be absent for a while. Do not wait for me.--D.

I am glad you found your way in here, for I am sure there is much that
will interest you. These companions

have been good friends to me, and for some years past, ever
since I had the idea of going to London, have given me many, many hours
of pleasure. Through them I have come to know your great England; and to
know her is to love her. I long to go through the crowded streets of
your mighty London, to be in the midst of the whirl and rush of
humanity, to share its life, its change, its death, and all that makes
it what it is. But alas! as yet I only know your tongue through books.
To you, my friend, I look that I know it to speak.
you know and speak English thoroughly!

I thank you, my friend, for your all too-flattering estimate, but yet I
fear that I am but a little way on the road I would travel. True, I know
the grammar and the words, but yet I know not how to speak them.

Well, I know that, did I move and speak in your
London, none there are who would not know me for a stranger. That is not
enough for me. Here I am noble; I am _boyar_; the common people know me,
and I am master. But a stranger in a strange land, he is no one; men
know him not--and to know not is to care not for. I am content if I am
like the rest, so that no man stops if he see me, or pause in his
speaking if he hear my words, 'Ha, ha! a stranger!' I have been so long
master that I would be master still--or at least that none other should
be master of me. You come to me not alone as agent of my friend Peter
Falk, of Elmsworth, to tell me all about my new estate in London. You
shall, I trust, rest here with me awhile, so that by our talking I may
learn the English intonation; and I would that you tell me when I make
error, even of the smallest, in my speaking. I am sorry that I had to be
away so long to-day; but you will, I know, forgive one who has so many
important affairs in hand.

You may go anywhere you wish in the castle, except where the doors are
locked, where of course you will not wish to go. There is reason that
all things are as they are, and did you see with my eyes and know with
my knowledge, you would perhaps better understand.

We are in Vardarania; and Vardarania is not England. Our ways are
not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things. Nay, from
what you have told me of your experiences already, you know something of
what strange things there may be.

in the region through which you came last night, there can be

was triumphant he found but little, for whatever there was had been
sheltered in the friendly soil.

Well, but, my friend, is it not needful that I should? When I go there
I shall be all alone, and my friend Kerr Aldous--nay, pardon me, I
fall into my country's habit of putting your patronymic first--my friend
Aldous Kerr will not be by my side to correct and aid me. He will be
in Elmsworth, miles away, probably working at papers of the law with my
other friend, Peter Falk. So!

At Purfleet, on a by-road, I came across just such a place as seemed to
be required, and where was displayed a dilapidated notice that the place
was for sale. It is surrounded by a high wall, of ancient structure,
built of heavy stones, and has not been repaired for a large number of
years. The closed gates are of heavy old oak and iron, all eaten with
rust.

The estate is called Carfell, no doubt a corruption of the old _Quatre
Face_, as the house is four-sided, agreeing with the cardinal points of
the compass. It contains in all some twenty acres, quite surrounded by
the solid stone wall above mentioned. There are many trees on it, which
make it in places gloomy, and there is a deep, dark-looking pond or
small lake, evidently fed by some springs, as the water is clear and
flows away in a fair-sized stream. The house is very large and of all
periods back, I should say, to mediæval times, for one part is of stone
immensely thick, with only a few windows high up and heavily barred with
iron. It looks like part of a keep, and is close to an old chapel or
church. I could not enter it, as I had not the key of the door leading
to it from the house, but I have taken with my kodak views of it from
various points. The house has been added to, but in a very straggling
way, and I can only guess at the amount of ground it covers, which must
be very great. There are but few houses close at hand, one being a very
large house only recently added to and formed into a private lunatic
asylum. It is not, however, visible from the grounds.

I am glad that it is old and big. I myself am of an old family, and to
live in a new house would kill me. A house cannot be made habitable in a
day; and, after all, how few days go to make up a century. I rejoice
also that there is a chapel of old times. We Transylvanian nobles love
not to think that our bones may lie amongst the common dead. I seek not
gaiety nor mirth, not the bright voluptuousness of much sunshine and
sparkling waters which please the young and gay. I am no longer young;
and my heart, through weary years of mourning over the dead, is not
attuned to mirth. Moreover, the walls of my castle are broken; the
shadows are many, and the wind breathes cold through the broken
battlements and casements. I love the shade and the shadow, and would
be alone with my thoughts when I may.

Forgive my long delay in writing, but I have been simply overwhelmed
with work. The life of an assistant schoolmistress is sometimes trying.
I am longing to be with you, and by the sea, where we can talk together
freely and build our castles in the air. I have been working very hard
lately, because I want to keep up with Aldous's studies, and I have
been practising shorthand very assiduously. When we are married I shall
be able to be useful to Aldous, and if I can stenograph well enough I
can take down what he wants to say in this way and write it out for
him on the typewriter, at which also I am practising very hard. He
and I sometimes write letters in shorthand, and he is keeping a
stenographic journal of his travels abroad. When I am with you I
shall keep a diary in the same way. I don't mean one of those
two-pages-to-the-week-with-Sunday-squeezed-in-a-corner diaries, but a
sort of journal which I can write in whenever I feel inclined. I do not
suppose there will be much of interest to other people; but it is not
intended for them. I may show it to Aldous some day if there is in it
anything worth sharing, but it is really an exercise book. I shall try
to do what I see lady journalists do: interviewing and writing
descriptions and trying to remember conversations. I am told that, with
a little practice, one can remember all that goes on or that one hears
said during a day. However, we shall see. I will tell you of my little
plans when we meet. I have just had a few hurried lines from Aldous
from Vardarania. He is well, and will be returning in about a week. I
am longing to hear all his news. It must be so nice to see strange
countries. I wonder if we--I mean Aldous and I--shall ever see them
together. There is the ten o'clock bell ringing. Good-bye.

Tell me all the news when you write. You have not told me anything for
a long time. I hear rumours, and especially of a tall, handsome,
curly-haired man???

I must say you tax me _very_ unfairly with being a bad correspondent. I
wrote to you _twice_ since we parted, and your last letter was only your
_second_. Besides, I have nothing to tell you. There is really nothing
to interest you. Town is very pleasant just now, and we go a good deal
to picture-galleries and for walks and rides in the park. As to the
tall, curly-haired man, I suppose it was the one who was with me at the
last Pop. Some one has evidently been telling tales. That was Mr.
Alderton. He often comes to see us, and he and mamma get on very well
together; they have so many things to talk about in common. We met some
time ago a man that would just _do for you_, if you were not already
engaged to Aldous. He is an excellent _parti_, being handsome, well
off, and of good birth. He is a doctor and really clever. Just fancy! He
is only nine-and-twenty, and he has an immense lunatic asylum all under
his own care. Mr. Alderton introduced him to me, and he called here to
see us, and often comes now. I think he is one of the most resolute men
I ever saw, and yet the most calm. He seems absolutely imperturbable. I
can fancy what a wonderful power he must have over his patients. He has
a curious habit of looking one straight in the face, as if trying to
read one's thoughts. He tries this on very much with me, but I flatter
myself he has got a tough nut to crack. I know that from my glass. Do
you ever try to read your own face? _I do_, and I can tell you it is not
a bad study, and gives you more trouble than you can well fancy if you
have never tried it. He says that I afford him a curious psychological
study, and I humbly think I do. I do not, as you know, take sufficient
interest in dress to be able to describe the new fashions. Dress is a
bore. That is slang again, but never mind; Percy says that every day.
There, it is all out. Nora, we have told all our secrets to each other
since we were _children_; we have slept together and eaten together, and
laughed and cried together; and now, though I have spoken, I would like
to speak more. Oh, Nora, couldn't you guess? I love him. I am blushing
as I write, for although I _think_ he loves me, he has not told me so in
words. But oh, Nora, I love him; I love him; I love him! There, that
does me good. I wish I were with you, dear, sitting by the fire
undressing, as we used to sit; and I would try to tell you what I feel.
I do not know how I am writing this even to you. I am afraid to stop,
or I should tear up the letter, and I don't want to stop, for I _do_ so
want to tell you all. Let me hear from you _at once_, and tell me all
that you think about it. Nora, I must stop. Good-night. Bless me in your
prayers; and, Nora, pray for my happiness.
P.S.--I need not tell you this is a secret. Good-night again.

Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so
nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

My dear, it never rains but it pours. How true the old proverbs are.
Here am I, who shall be twenty in September, and yet I never had a
proposal till to-day, not a real proposal, and to-day I have had three.
Just fancy! THREE proposals in one day! Isn't it awful! I feel sorry,
really and truly sorry, for two of the poor fellows. Oh, Nora, I am so
happy that I don't know what to do with myself. And three proposals!
But, for goodness' sake, don't tell any of the girls, or they would be
getting all sorts of extravagant ideas and imagining themselves injured
and slighted if in their very first day at home they did not get six at
least. Some girls are so vain! You and I, Nora dear, who are engaged and
are going to settle down soon soberly into old married women, can
despise vanity. Well, I must tell you about the three, but you must keep
it a secret, dear, from _every one_, except, of course, Aldous. You
will tell him, because I would, if I were in your place, certainly tell
Percy. A woman ought to tell her husband everything--don't you think
so, dear?--and I must be fair. Men like women, certainly their wives, to
be quite as fair as they are; and women, I am afraid, are not always
quite as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, number One came just
before lunch. I told you of him, Dr. Elias Ward, the lunatic-asylum
man, with the strong jaw and the good forehead. He was very cool
outwardly, but was nervous all the same. He had evidently been schooling
himself as to all sorts of little things, and remembered them; but he
almost managed to sit down on his silk hat, which men don't generally do
when they are cool, and then when he wanted to appear at ease he kept
playing with a lancet in a way that made me nearly scream. He spoke to
me, Nora, very straightforwardly. He told me how dear I was to him,
though he had known me so little, and what his life would be with me to
help and cheer him. He was going to tell me how unhappy he would be if I
did not care for him, but when he saw me cry he said that he was a brute
and would not add to my present trouble. Then he broke off and asked if
I could love him in time; and when I shook my head his hands trembled,
and then with some hesitation he asked me if I cared already for any one
else. He put it very nicely, saying that he did not want to wring my
confidence from me, but only to know, because if a woman's heart was
free a man might have hope. And then, Nora, I felt a sort of duty to
tell him that there was some one. I only told him that much, and then he
stood up, and he looked very strong and very grave as he took both my
hands in his and said he hoped I would be happy, and that if I ever
wanted a friend I must count him one of my best. Oh, Nora dear, I can't
help crying: and you must excuse this letter being all blotted. Being
proposed to is all very nice and all that sort of thing, but it isn't at
all a happy thing when you have to see a poor fellow, whom you know
loves you honestly, going away and looking all broken-hearted, and to
know that, no matter what he may say at the moment, you are passing
quite out of his life. My dear, I must stop here at present, I feel so
miserable, though I am so happy.

Percy has just gone, and I feel in better spirits than when I left
off, so I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, number Two
came after lunch. He is such a nice fellow, an American from Texas, and
he looks so young and so fresh that it seems almost impossible that he
has been to so many places and has had such adventures. I sympathise
with poor Desdemona when she had such a dangerous stream poured in her
ear, even by a black man. I suppose that we women are such cowards that
we think a man will save us from fears, and we marry him. I know now
what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I
don't, for there was Mr. Boone telling us his stories, and Percy never
told any, and yet---- My dear, I am somewhat previous. Mr. Cassidy P.
Boone found me alone. It seems that a man always does find a girl
alone. No, he doesn't, for Percy tried twice to _make_ a chance, and I
helping him all I could; I am not ashamed to say it now. I must tell you
beforehand that Mr. Boone doesn't always speak slang--that is to say,
he never does so to strangers or before them, for he is really well
educated and has exquisite manners--but he found out that it amused me
to hear him talk American slang, and whenever I was present, and there
was no one to be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my
dear, he has to invent it all, for it fits exactly into whatever else he
has to say. But this is a way slang has. I do not know myself if I shall
ever speak slang; I do not know if Percy likes it, as I have never
heard him use any as yet. Well, Mr. Boone sat down beside me and looked
as happy and jolly as he could, but I could see all the same that he was
very nervous. He took my hand in his, and said ever so sweetly:--

'Miss Cora, I know I ain't good enough to regulate the fixin's of your
little shoes, but I guess if you wait till you find a man that is you
will go join them seven young women with the lamps when you quit. Won't
you just hitch up alongside of me and let us go down the long road
together, driving in double harness?'

Well, he did look so good-humoured and so jolly that it didn't seem
half so hard to refuse him as it did poor Dr. Ward; so I said, as
lightly as I could, that I did not know anything of hitching, and that I
wasn't broken to harness at all yet. Then he said that he had spoken in
a light manner, and he hoped that if he had made a mistake in doing so
on so grave, so momentous, an occasion for him, I would forgive him. He
really did look serious when he was saying it, and I couldn't help
feeling a bit serious too--I know, Nora, you will think me a horrid
flirt--though I couldn't help feeling a sort of exultation that he was
number two in one day. And then, my dear, before I could say a word he
began pouring out a perfect torrent of love-making, laying his very
heart and soul at my feet. He looked so earnest over it that I shall
never again think that a man must be playful always, and never earnest,
because he is merry at times. I suppose he saw something in my face
which checked him, for he suddenly stopped, and said with a sort of
manly fervour that I could have loved him for if I had been free:--

'Cora, you are an honest-hearted girl, I know. I should not be here
speaking to you as I am now if I did not believe you clean grit, right
through to the very depths of your soul. Tell me, like one good fellow
to another, is there any one else that you care for? And if there is
I'll never trouble you a hair's breadth again, but will be, if you will
let me, a very faithful friend.'

My dear Nora, why are men so noble when we women are so little worthy
of them? Here was I almost making fun of this great-hearted, true
gentleman. I burst into tears--I am afraid, my dear, you will think
this a very sloppy letter in more ways than one--and I really felt very
badly. Why can't they let a girl marry three men, or as many as want
her, and save all this trouble? But this is heresy, and I must not say
it. I am glad to say that, though I was crying, I was able to look into
Mr. Boone's brave eyes, and I told him out straight:--

'Yes, there is some one I love, though he has not told me yet that he
even loves me.' I was right to speak to him so frankly, for quite a
light came into his face, and he put out both his hands and took mine--I
think I put them into his--and said in a hearty way:--

'That's my brave girl. It's better worth being late for a chance of
winning you than being in time for any other girl in the world. Don't
cry, my dear. If it's for me, I'm a hard nut to crack; and I take it
standing up. If that other fellow doesn't know his happiness, well, he'd
better look for it soon, or he'll have to deal with me. Little girl,
your honesty and pluck have made me a friend, and that's rarer than a
lover; it's more unselfish anyhow. My dear, I'm going to have a pretty
lonely walk between this and Kingdom Come. Won't you give me one kiss?
It'll be something to keep off the darkness now and then. You can, you
know, if you like, for that other good fellow--he must be a good fellow,
my dear, and a fine fellow, or you could not love him--hasn't spoken
yet.' That quite won me, Nora, for it _was_ brave and sweet of him, and
noble, too, to a rival--wasn't it?--and he so sad; so I leant over and
kissed him. He stood up with my two hands in his, and as he looked down
into my face--I am afraid I was blushing very much--he said:--

'Little girl, I hold your hand, and you've kissed me, and if these
things don't make us friends nothing ever will. Thank you for your sweet
honesty to me, and good-bye.' He wrung my hand, and taking up his hat,
went straight out of the room without looking back, without a tear or a
quiver or a pause; and I am crying like a baby. Oh, why must a man like
that be made unhappy when there are lots of girls about who would
worship the very ground he trod on? I know I would if I were free--only
I don't want to be free. My dear, this quite upset me, and I feel I
cannot write of happiness just at once, after telling you of it; and I
don't wish to tell of the number three until it can be all happy.

P.S.--Oh, about number Three--I needn't tell you of number Three, need
I? Besides, it was all so confused; it seemed only a moment from his
coming into the room till both his arms were round me, and he was
kissing me. I am very, very happy, and I don't know what I have done to
deserve it. I must only try in the future to show that I am not
ungrateful to God for all His goodness to me in sending to me such a
lover, such a husband, and such a friend.

My poor little feet didn't make much noise then! I daresay poor old Mr.
Swales would have told me that it was because I didn't want to wake up
Geordie.

I didn't quite dream; but it all seemed to be real. I only wanted to be
here in this spot--I don't know why, for I was afraid of something--I
don't know what. I remember, though I suppose I was asleep, passing
through the streets and over the bridge. A fish leaped as I went by, and
I leaned over to look at it, and I heard a lot of dogs howling--the
whole town seemed as if it must be full of dogs all howling at once--as
